s08.slug: THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 11 · 1:00 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 → 11:10 PM · THE ANCHOR
body: The sun reaches the window end of 302 at five past one and lies down the varnish in a bright slab, with the last chair in the middle of it, empty. The table has stopped using that chair out of something like manners: the two window girls have shifted a seat down, Yusuf’s cup keeps to its own end, and Caleb has hung his backpack on the next chair so that the strap makes a velvet rope. It’s a molded beige chair with a gouge in one arm, and it is, Jack decides, the most influential person in the room.
Evan has the roster at the door. Over his head, on the whiteboard, in Hale’s tilted hand: HAPPY BIRTHDAY MR. MARSH — DO NOT SING. Caleb’s mouth is already open on the first syllable.
“Mr. Hargrove,” says Hale, coming in with a paperback under his arm and a coffee he looks to be regretting, and Caleb’s mouth closes.
“Thirty,” Evan says to the roster. “Thirty is when they stop calling it ABD and start calling it a lifestyle.” He ticks off Jack’s name and moves on to Yusuf’s.

“At thirty I owned one coat and an opinion of Hume I have since had to retire,” Hale tells the table, taking the middle of the long side, where he can turn his head to either end. “Mr. Marsh has the better of me: he’s employed. We are done with Waugh. Mr. Costigan, the last page. I have a dean at half past two, and the man has not improved.”
Jack addresses the chair, currently Hale. “The lamp at the end isn’t the answer, Professor. It’s a light somebody left on.”

Hale turns down the length of the table to the window end, out of a habit that is a week old, and says to the beige chair in the sun, “Miss Broussard, Mr. Costigan contends that the lamp is not the answer but a light left on —”
He stops.
“The chair,” Hale says, and hears it. “The chair is… addressing furniture.” He keeps his eyes on the empty seat until Caleb coughs. “Carry on.”
Jack has the rebuttal to the rebuttal built already, and it’s a good one, with a hinge in the middle of it, and there’s nowhere to take it. It sits in him, hot, till the hour is out.

At ten to two Hale holds up the paperback, a green Penguin gone soft at the spine. “Greene. *The End of the Affair.* For Monday the twenty-second, when the table will once again be in a position to contradict me.” He opens it and reads: “A story has no beginning or end: arbitrarily one chooses that moment of experience from which to look back or from which to look ahead.”
“The narrator tells you in a few pages that this is a record of hatred, more than of love,” he says, and shuts it. “He’s lying, the poor sod. Catch him at it.”
Caleb writes the first line down, colon and all. Jack doesn’t. He is going to buy the book.

By ten past eleven the Anchor is down to its night people: the harbor black in the windows, the pie case three-quarters gone, and on the end stool Merle with a bowl of chowder and a dollar’s worth of jukebox. The machine is playing the one Mariah Carey song it owns. No one has ever been caught choosing it. From the back booth, when it ends, comes a single “Brava,” and Merle looks up to see who’s being praised.

Hale has taken Evan to the back booth for his birthday. At the pass Gloria pins a ticket to the rail with the flat of her hand. “Two professors in my booth on a Thursday,” she says. “I’ll need a priest.”
“I can get you one,” Jack says. “He keeps Wednesday hours.”
“I need him tonight, hon. Wednesday’s no good to me.” She goes off with the pot.

Twenty minutes on, a plate comes back through the pass with a slice of olallieberry on it, cut by somebody with views on the angle. “From the booth,” Gloria says. “The one with the wine on his cuff. That’s my nine, hon. Eat it before the dishes find you.”

Jack eats it standing at the Hobart with the steam in his face, and through the pass he gets the booth in slices. Hale is on his third, house red in a juice glass, and is explaining something to the sugar dispenser with both hands. Evan has had coffee, and then coffee, and has thanked Gloria both times. When the third glass comes down Evan looks at it, and at the clock over the pie case, and back at his cup. Hale doesn’t see him do it.

At a quarter to one Hale pays at the register, and Jack, passing with a bus tub on his hip, hears his name. “Mr. Costigan.” Evan has already gone out to unlock his bike. Hale lays a twenty on a check about half that and doesn’t wait for change. “The table is very quiet, Mr. Costigan. I find I miss being contradicted.”
“I could contradict you now, Professor.”
“Not at this hour,” Hale says, getting an arm into his coat. “I’d only agree with you.” He goes out into the fog buttoned wrong by one.
Gloria wipes the counter down to the grain. “When’s she back?”
“The twenty-first. Sunday night.”

body.text: “Then you’ll want the Saturday before to clean your room,” Gloria says. “Take it. Go get your peach. Rudy’ll cover the Hobart.”
body.else: “Then you’ll want the Saturday before to clean your room,” Gloria says. “Take it. Go get your girl. Rudy’ll cover the Hobart.”

body: From the grill, without turning around, Rudy says, “No.”
“He means yes,” Gloria says.
Friday night, on his way down to the laundry, Jack finds a new laminate on the Fishbowl door.

body.title: Laminate, on the Fishbowl door
body.text:
OLYMPIC VIEWING
PER THE RESIDENTIAL LIFE HANDBOOK, NO CHANTING

body: Inside, the lounge television has the opening ceremony on, in the rain: a pickup truck in Vancouver with Wayne Gretzky standing in the bed, soaked to the collar and waving, on his way to light a cauldron outdoors. Doug, from the arm of the couch: “U-S-A.”
“Douglas,” says Priya, from the doorway, and taps the laminate.

journal.title: Evan Marsh (TA)
journal.text: Thursday section, Hollis 108. Kierkegaard. Kind to the scared ones, murder on the lazy ones. Smokes American Spirits. Rides a bike. Came back from PERSONAL grayer. Told us we’d left out a driver. Says Kierkegaard was engaged once, gave back the ring, and wrote about her for the rest of his life. Gave back the midterms, then read us Kierkegaard on recollecting the dead — the freest love, because they can’t pay you back. Couldn’t finish the paragraph. After the last section: the man in the white jacket. Was he at Preview Weekend last April? I don’t know. Don’t tell him I asked. I gave him Theo’s name. February eleventh he turned thirty. Thirty is when they stop calling it ABD and start calling it a lifestyle. Hale took him to the Anchor’s back booth on my shift and sent me a slice.

s08a.slug: SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 13 · 6:40 AM · CAMPUS POINT — PAIR FORTY-ONE
body: Sunrise is ten minutes off. The sky over the Channel has a seam of lemon along its underside, the one sodium lamp on the lot pole is still burning out of forgetfulness, and the bluff at Campus Point has nothing on it but gulls and Jack.

Pair 41 is one person this morning. Fenner’s form says STATION 2, over two columns, OBSERVER 1 and OBSERVER 2, each with a line for a name. The method hasn’t changed: pick a rock, time ten crests across it, write them down. The stopwatch is the department’s, PROPERTY OF MORRO 1100 scratched into its back with a key. Skye used to hold the pencil because she had the handwriting. The handwriting is all his today.

He does ten for COSTIGAN. Fenner has said no trades, and the form has a second column, so he does ten more for CALLENDER off the same rock, in the same square capitals, and on the line that says OBSERVER’S LOCATION he writes IN NEW MEXICO and reads it back. Her numbers agree with his to the second. Fenner is going to notice.
At two minutes past seven the RAZR goes off against the clipboard.

Yusuf is coming along the bluff path from the lot with a steel thermos, in the gray Marisol hoodie, at the pace of a man who has walked this path every morning for weeks. He walks at dawn now. He hasn’t said whose habit it is.
“It started last night,” Yusuf says, by way of hello, and takes the rail beside him with his eyes on the water. “Marjah. That’s when we heard. Over there it was already morning.”
Jack puts the pencil down on the clipboard. “Okay,” he says.

“Tariq’s been home since the twenty-third.” Yusuf unscrews the thermos. “He did the stairs, all fourteen, in January. Now he sits. My father bought a second television so they’d stop fighting over which channel, and now there are two, and they watch both.”
“Does he say anything?”

“They say it wrong. The anchors. Tariq corrects them, out loud, in a normal voice, to the screen, and then again in case they missed it. Dad turned the sound off the first night. Tariq turned it back on.” He pours tea into the thermos lid and watches it steam. “He knows the names of the roads.”
“My brother is home,” Yusuf says, “and he’s still over there.” He holds the lid out.
Jack takes it. It’s hot through the plastic.
“It’s tea,” Yusuf says. “Not coffee. I’m telling you now so there’s no face.”
It is black enough to read by and has cardamom in it. Jack drinks it down to the leaves. Yusuf reads the form over his shoulder.
“‘In New Mexico.’”
“It’s a location.”
“It’s a boundary condition,” Yusuf says, and holds out a hand for the stopwatch. “Give me that. I’ll call them. You write.”
They do ten. Yusuf calls the crests across the rock in the order they come, dry and unhurried, eleven, twelve, eleven, and Jack writes them down.
“Which column?” Yusuf asks, at the fourth.
“Hers,” Jack says, and writes it there in his own hand.

journal.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us. Broke the fast with his people on Mission Street and fed me till I couldn’t stand. Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks. His nineteenth, at Bastille, with a candle in a scone. He watched the memorial Tuesday. Standing up. I didn’t ask. The night of the West Point speech: ‘You left the first time. My father watched you leave. If you’re going to come, stay.’ His brother Tariq — an IED in Helmand. Alive. Germany. I went after him. We sat on the east stairs. Back for finals the night before Oslo. Tariq’s learning stairs. He’d like the speech to be right. Tariq home the twenty-third. Fourteen stairs; he’s done eleven. A fifth rail. February thirteenth, on the bluff at Campus Point at dawn, with a thermos: Marjah started last night. Tariq’s home and watching every channel. His brother is home, he says, and he’s still over there.

s09.slug: SUNDAY, FEBRUARY 14 · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S → DELGADO HALL, 412 — VALENTINE’S

body.text: At the 11:30 he goes up. It’s the first time since the Sunday before Candlemas, and he makes nothing of it: he takes it, goes back to the Joseph side, and kneels with his face in his hands, as Frank does in the third pew at St. Brigid’s. He has never noticed himself doing it.
body.else: At the 11:30 he stays in the pew, on the Joseph side, and the line goes up past his knees and comes back. Here people know to notice. Becca, three pews up, doesn’t turn around, and he is grateful to the back of her head.

body: The RAZR spends Mass on silent in the Carhartt, and in the courtyard it hands him two things.

body.text: Lion dance, 9:40 a.m., Mary Queen of Vietnam. Bà Nội called the priest from San Jose before Mass. He announced me. I’m told I’m “promising.”

body: The picture follows, red and gold: a lion’s head caught mid-leap, firecracker paper strewn across the asphalt under it like confetti. In Jack’s experience *promising* is what a parish calls you shortly before somebody hands you a clipboard.
He texts back *nice*. Nothing comes, and he takes it for *I know*.

412 is empty when he gets back up the hill, and it is empty all afternoon. Theo’s pillow is squared on a bed that hasn’t been slept in since the fifth. Around five the MacBook, which Jack has permission to open, opens to the News Feed.

body.name: Doug Pruitt
body.text: DREW BREES IS A KING NOW. like an actual king. of BACCHUS. dude

body: Doug has discovered that a quarterback can be a king, and has not recovered.
Ma calls at twenty past five, from the kitchen: a spoon on the rim of a pot, a cupboard, the dryer working at the bottom of the cellar stairs.

“The candle got as far as the lobby,” she says, no hello. “In a bag with his number on it. Same as every February. A man in a vest said it was a fire hazard. I said it was blessed on the second, and he said that’s not a defense, Mrs. Costigan, and I said it is in my house.”
“How is he?”

“One-eighty push-ups. He wanted you told. Not how he is. The number. He said, tell the Professor one-eighty. I said one-eighty what, and he said, Ma, just tell him.” A lid goes onto something. “And he got something in the mail from New Mexico. He wouldn’t say what. He was smiling like when he was nine and he had the frog in his pocket.”
Jack arranges his face for a telephone.
Behind her an extension picks up, and Frank breathes into the line once. “Saints,” he says. There’s a pause with a television in it. “Good for them. They suffered.” The extension clicks down.
From the front room, through two walls, Nonna says something with *la ragazza* in it, and something with *neve*.

“She wants to know is that the girl in the snow,” Ma says. “Gina looked it up, Jackie, Santa Fe, she printed the weather and it’s on the refrigerator under the Saints magnet. Nonna lit the Candelora candle for her. *Per la neve.* I said Ma, it’s the fourteenth, Candlemas was the second. She said a candle doesn’t read the calendar.”

body.text: At the end her voice goes quieter. “Are you still the happiest you’ve been all year?”
body.else: At the end she says, “Eat something, Jackie. It’s Sunday.”

body.text: “Good,” Ma says, and the line is quiet long enough for the word to be the other thing, too.

body: At half past six Theo files his dispatches.

body.text: The harpist at Laney’s party. She is also, it emerges, a notary. She witnessed a document for Tony between sets.

body: Under it, once it finishes loading: a woman at a gold harp beneath a crystal chandelier, mid-glissando, a fountain pen behind one ear. The harpist is a notary, exactly as pitched, and is being reported as a discovery.

body.text: Celeste’s cake. Nineteen candles and a fleur-de-lis in buttercream. Laney wept into it. Do not tell her I told you.

body: The picture is a white cake with a field of small flames on it. He counts them. Nineteen. At the edge of the frame there’s a hand and a cuff he would know in a lineup, holding a fork. He checks the other corners: a doily, the rim of a plate, a piece of tablecloth.
By nine there is nothing left to do in 412 but the last Post-it in the stack, as promised.

body.title: Yellow Post-it, fountain pen, on a DVD spine

body: On the screen a man strains spaghetti through a tennis racket. Jack’s grandmother’s views on colanders, available in Calabrian, play over the scene on a separate track. Afterward a man and a woman play gin. The last thing anyone says in the picture is *Shut up and deal*, with the cards in her hand, and then it simply stops, and Jack sits on the end of his bed with the credits going up and the lamp off.
By the RAZR’s clock it is still Laney’s birthday for another half hour. He has had it open to her name since the credits.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’ Sunday, after the 8:00 and Trumbull: Father Dom said a prophet’s never welcome at home, and Pop said that’s for sure in the pew. She’d seen the taco picture: *she’s tiny.* Then one question — did I go up today. I said yes. She said good. Candlemas, from the vestibule: Danny’s twenty-three. Two letters beats one card. Wednesday she called about the song. Rita Pallante’s youngest showed Rita, and Rita showed the parish kitchen. Pop told her it’s about a birthday. She asked me one thing: is she good to me. Then: it’s Wednesday, Jackie. Valentine’s, after Trumbull: the candle got as far as the lobby, in a bag with Danny’s number, same as every February. One-eighty push-ups. He got something from New Mexico and wouldn’t say what. Pop came on the extension: Saints. Good for them. They suffered. Nonna lit her Candelora candle for the girl in the snow. Then Ma asked was I still the happiest I’ve been all year. I said yes. She said good.

choices.key: On Laney’s nineteenth birthday you texted her happy birthday.
response: His name. No *fireman*. It is the coldest thing she has ever sent him, and it has a period on it.

choices.text: *Text her:* “happy birthday. tell the harpist hi.”
choices.key: On Laney’s nineteenth birthday you texted her happy birthday and a joke about the harpist.

response.text: happy birthday. tell the harpist hi

response: The screen dims on that, and he lets it.

choices.key: On Laney’s nineteenth birthday you had Theo tell her for you.

response.text: Delivered. She said “how kind.” In the voice.

response: He knows the voice. It can make *how kind* last four seconds and cost a dollar.

choices.key: On Laney’s nineteenth birthday you sent nothing.
response: He shuts the RAZR on her name. On Theo’s desk the little travel clock goes on toward the fifteenth, which belongs to Kevin.
